analysis.one_liner: Extends overtime pay, paid sick days, written contracts, and break rights to the nation's domestic workers.
analysis.headline: The Domestic Workers Bill of Rights Act drew 131 House Democratic cosponsors but never received a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give the roughly 2.2 million people who clean homes, watch children, and care for seniors and people with disabilities a set of workplace rights most other workers already have. It would end the exemption that leaves live-in domestic workers without overtime pay, require written contracts covering pay, hours, and termination, guarantee paid sick days and meal and rest breaks, and bar employers from retaliating against workers who complain — including by threatening them with immigration reports. It would also extend federal anti-discrimination law to domestic workers and fund outreach, a complaint hotline, and higher Medicaid payments for home care.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 2.2 million domestic workers — nannies, housekeepers, home health and personal care aides — nine in ten of whom are women, disproportionately women of color and immigrants, earning an average of about $13.79 an hour. They would gain overtime pay, paid sick time, written contracts, break rights, scheduling protections, and enforceable retaliation protections. Families who rely on their care would also benefit from reduced turnover.
analysis.who_benefits_short: 2.2 million nannies, cleaners, and home care aides

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Fair Labor Standards Act provision that exempts live-in domestic workers from overtime pay, and requires 30 days of lodging or two weeks' severance pay when a live-in worker is terminated.

Requires a signed written agreement, in plain language, for any domestic employee working 8 or more hours a week, covering pay rate, hours, breaks, termination policies, and grievance procedures, and bars forced arbitration and noncompete clauses in those agreements.

Guarantees one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year, usable for the worker's own illness, caring for family, or escaping domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.

Requires meal breaks after 5 hours and 10-minute rest breaks every 4 hours, 72-hour notice of schedule changes, pay for cancelled scheduled hours, and protections against being monitored in private spaces or having wages docked for breakage or losses.

Amends Title VII of the Civil Rights Act to cover domestic employees, who are largely excluded today because of small-employer thresholds and misclassification as contractors, and prohibits retaliation — including reporting or threatening to report a worker's immigration status — with a presumption of retaliation when a worker is fired within 90 days of asserting a right.

Creates a Domestic Employee Standards Board, a national complaint hotline, grants for community outreach and enforcement, an interagency enforcement task force, and a temporary increase in the federal Medicaid matching rate for home care services provided by domestic workers.

analysis.who_pays: The households that employ nannies, housekeepers, and aides — including middle-class families as well as affluent ones — would bear overtime, sick pay, severance, and scheduling-compliance costs, and home care agencies would face contracting and scheduling requirements. The federal government would absorb higher Medicaid matching payments, and the bill authorizes new appropriations for the hotline, grants, and standards board.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households and agencies that employ domestic workers

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden falls heavily on individual households rather than large firms: any family employing a nanny or aide 8 hours a week would need written agreements, scheduling notices at least 72 hours in advance, sick-time accounting, and termination payments — paperwork and costs that could push some families toward informal, unregulated arrangements instead.

Overtime and scheduling pay for live-in and in-home care raise the cost of caring for elderly and disabled people at home; the bill tries to soften this with a two-year phase-in, delayed enforcement for government-funded programs, and higher federal Medicaid payments, but states and families would still shoulder part of the cost.

Employing a domestic worker would carry new legal exposure — liquidated damages for severance violations, up to $2,000 per violation of communication rules, and a presumption of retaliation after a complaint — which an honest supporter must weigh against the isolation and powerlessness that made such protections the bill's purpose.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and go to a workforce that the bill's findings document as earning about $13.79 an hour, largely without contracts, benefits, or legal protection — 91 percent of workers who faced problems in one study said they did not complain for fear of losing their job. The costs, while genuine, are the ordinary cost of extending labor standards: higher pay and scheduling obligations for employers, mostly individual households. The bill's own design acknowledges the strain on care recipients by phasing in rules over two years, exempting shared living arrangements, and adding federal Medicaid money. The main honest objection is that compliance is hardest for exactly the small, informal arrangements the bill covers, so some work could shift underground.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to six House committees the day it was introduced, none of them ever took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the Domestic Workers Bill of Rights Act in the House on June 13, 2024.

On the day of introduction it was referred to six committees — Education and the Workforce, House Administration, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Oversight and Accountability, and Judiciary — 'for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker.'
131 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; the record shows no further committee or floor action of any kind after the referral.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and bills not acted on die with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households, care agencies, and platforms that employ domestic workers avoided overtime, sick pay, contract, and scheduling requirements, and federal Medicaid spending was spared the bill's matching-rate increase. The 2.2 million domestic workers the bill covered gained nothing, since no state-level or federal replacement was enacted in its place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers of domestic workers, who face no new rules

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Domestic Workers Bill of Rights Act in the House on June 13, 2024.

for.name: 131 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the support of a majority of the House Democratic caucus, but no member brought it to the floor.

for.name: National Domestic Workers Alliance
for.what_they_did: The long-standing national campaign for domestic worker rights legislation; the bill's findings rest heavily on NDWA studies of working conditions and pandemic-era job loss.

against.name: House committees of referral (6)
against.role: Education and the Workforce, House Administration, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Oversight and Accountability, and Judiciary Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 13, 2024 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill never left committee.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority controlling the House floor and committee agendas
against.what_they_did: Brought the bill no further than referral; no committee consideration or floor action occurred during the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 131 cosponsors were Democrats, roughly 61 percent of the House Democratic caucus; the record shows no Republican cosponsors and the bill never advanced in the Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: Families employing nannies, cleaners, and aides would owe overtime, paid sick time, written contracts, scheduling pay, and severance for live-in workers. These costs fall directly on the employers of the workers the bill protects, from affluent households to middle-class ones.

industries.industry: Home care and personal care agencies
industries.note: Agencies would face contract, scheduling, and wage obligations for their aides, but the bill's temporary increase in the federal Medicaid matching rate would channel more federal money into Medicaid-funded home care that many of the same agencies provide.

The bill bars employers from docking pay or penalizing workers who communicate directly with clients rather than through the platform's app, and requires written agreements that displace opaque app terms. Platforms profit today from informal, low-accountability arrangements.

industries.industry: State Medicaid home and community-based care programs
industries.note: A temporary federal medical assistance percentage increase would offset part of the cost of applying the new standards to Medicaid-funded home care, lowering the state share while raising what aides are entitled to.
